title: Space Weapons: First Ask Where They Are
part1:
When you hear “space weapons,” it may sound like one kind of weapon. But the key to understanding this news is not to imagine what the weapons can do. It is to ask, “Where are they?” and check their address.

In September 2026, the U.S. Secretary of the Air Force said that the United States was deploying space-control weapons in orbit to protect the Joint Force from the actions of hostile parties. An official article by a U.S. government agency records this as the first statement to acknowledge the Space Force’s deployment of weapons. However, the weapons’ names, ability to attack, and targets were not made clear. All we know is that they are being deployed in orbit.
part2:
It is important not to mix this up with a missile launched from the ground to attack a satellite. In 2021, Russia fired a missile from the ground and destroyed a satellite. More than 1,500 pieces of debris could be tracked. That was a case of targeting space from the ground. This announcement is about deploying weapons in orbit. The difference is not only whether the target is in space; the weapons are in different places, too.

Also, “conflict over space” does not refer only to weapons in orbit. The U.S. Space Force’s 2025 operational framework covers attacks and defenses in orbit, across communication links, and at ground locations. Electromagnetic attacks on communications and cyberattacks are included, too. On the other hand, warning about threats, making equipment harder to damage, and spreading out functions are defensive steps. We should avoid mixing these up with putting attack weapons in orbit.
part3:
It is easy to get the treaty’s limits wrong if we sum them up in one phrase. Article IV of the Outer Space Treaty bans placing objects carrying nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit around Earth. It also bans putting such weapons on celestial bodies or deploying them in outer space in other ways. On celestial bodies, it also bans military bases and forts, weapons tests, and military exercises. This does not mean that the treaty has a rule banning all conventional weapons from orbit.

When you see a headline about “space weapons,” first check their address. Are they in orbit, on the ground, or within communications? There may be one label, but the things it covers belong to several different categories.
in_one_line: The key to understanding space weapons is asking where they are, not just what they can do.
